title: Mastering the Third Dimension With Atomic Layer Etch
summary: As AI pushes chips into taller, more complex 3D structures, removing material from the top down isn't enough anymore. Harmeet Singh explains how atomic layer etch makes precise processing from the side possible.

- AI demand is driving chips into increasingly complex 3D architectures.
- Thermal chemical atomic layer etch (ALE) enables precise lateral processing inside hard-to-reach structures.


The industry is entering an exciting new chapter in semiconductor scaling. From 3D NAND and advanced logic architectures to next-generation DRAM and advanced packaging, chipmakers are adopting increasingly complex three-dimensional structures to improve performance, density, and energy efficiency.


This transition creates a new manufacturing challenge: controlling material removal not only from the top down, but also laterally. As 3D architectures become more advanced, lateral etch is emerging as a critical capability for enabling the next generation of logic and memory.


*Left to right: 3D NAND continues to add layers, increasing the depth and complexity of device structures. Advanced logic is progressing from FinFET to gate-all-around architectures, with complementary FET structures on the horizon, and DRAM technologies are exploring new three-dimensional designs to achieve greater density.*


### 3D Device Architectures Require New Approaches


For years, semiconductor manufacturing relied primarily on directional, top-down patterning. These techniques enabled remarkable progress as devices became smaller and feature counts increased.


As device structures grow taller, more complex, and more interconnected, top-down patterning remains essential, but it is no longer sufficient on its own. Conventional reactive ion etch (RIE) is highly effective for directional, top-down processing, but directional ions do not naturally move laterally (i.e., sideways) through intricate geometries.


As a result, device manufacturers need new ways to shape, thin, and recess materials inside these structures.


Lam is focused on solving these manufacturing challenges through continued innovation in etch, deposition, plasma, and surface chemistry.


### Atomic Layer Etch Enables Precision Inside Complex Structures


Atomic layer etch, or ALE, uses controlled surface reactions to modify a thin layer of material, then selectively remove it. The process shares many of the same scientific principles with atomic layer deposition (ALD).


In contrast to ALD, which has benefited from decades of development, thermal chemical ALE is still an emerging capability. This makes it an important moment for innovation in chemistry, process technology, equipment design, modeling, and device integration.


### Turning Atomic-Scale Science Into Manufacturing Solutions


At Lam Research, we are advancing ALE approaches aimed at three key lateral-processing challenges:


- **Film thinning:** Reducing film thickness with atomic-scale control while maintaining smooth, low-defect surfaces. A key application is scaling high-aspect-ratio devices to increasingly smaller critical dimensions.
- **Trimming and shaping:** Controlling the dimensions and geometry of complex device features. This includes shaping 3D structures that require lateral in addition to vertical processing.
- **Selective lateral recess:** Removing a controlled amount of a targeted material while preserving surrounding materials. For gapfill materials, this requires recessing without seam expansion and maintaining excellent profile control from top to bottom.


All three approaches require consistent removal of the right amount of material, in the right places, with highest selectivity and no loss of surrounding materials. They must also deliver the performance and productivity required for high-volume manufacturing.


As semiconductor scaling drives increasingly complex structures, materials, and process windows, innovation can no longer rely on experimentation alone. At Lam, we are expanding our fundamental understanding to move from experiment-based process development toward more predictive approaches. Our work spans large-scale modeling and atomic-level understanding of surface chemistry to build a stronger scientific foundation for faster discovery and optimization of next-generation semiconductor processes.


### Advancing ALE Through Ecosystem Collaboration


Closing those gaps will require collaboration across the semiconductor ecosystem. Thermal chemical ALE sits at the intersection of materials science, surface chemistry, process technology, equipment design, modeling, and device integration. Progress depends on close coordination among device makers, equipment suppliers, academia, and research partners.


Lam has played a leading role in collaborating with these groups on the manufacturing challenges that matter most for next-generation logic and memory. By combining deep expertise in etch, deposition, plasma, and surface chemistry with close engagement across the research community, Lam is helping translate atomic-scale science into repeatable, high-volume manufacturing solutions.


### FAQ


**What is atomic layer etch (ALE)?**


Atomic layer etch is a materials-processing technique that removes material through controlled, self-limiting surface reactions. It is designed to provide highly precise material removal for advanced semiconductor structures.


**Why is atomic layer etch important for 3D semiconductor devices?**


As device structures become taller and more complex, manufacturers must process materials in both vertical and lateral dimensions. ALE can help shape, thin, or recess materials inside structures that conventional directional etch processes may have difficulty reaching.


**How is thermal chemical atomic layer etch different from conventional plasma etch?**


Conventional plasma etch often removes material continuously and directionally. Thermal chemical ALE divides the process into controlled surface-modification and removal steps, enabling more precise control over the amount of material removed. This enables zero ion damage and provides high selectivity to minimize loss of underlying integration stack materials.


**Which semiconductor devices benefit from atomic layer etch?**


Potential applications include 3D NAND, gate-all-around logic, next-generation memory, advanced packaging, and other architectures that require highly selective, atomic-scale material control.


**How is Lam approaching atomic layer etch?**


Lam’s approach to ALE is to connect atomic-scale science with high-volume manufacturing. We combine process engineering with deep expertise in surface chemistry, kinetics, transport, equipment and process integration. These capabilities allow the delivery of precise, selective material removal at the productivity required for increasingly complex 3D devices.


**Why is modeling important for atomic layer etch?**


ALE involves complex interactions between reactant transport, surface chemistry, reaction kinetics, and material removal. Modeling helps connect these different scales and provides deeper insight into the mechanisms that control selectivity, uniformity, etch rate, and self-limiting behavior.


**Can modeling help reduce experimental learning cycles?**


That is an important opportunity. By combining first-principles understanding, multiscale modeling, experimental data, and AI, we can increasingly use simulation to identify promising chemistry and process regimes before committing extensive experimental resources.
